composition_notes: Keep the investigation centered on conservation practice, room-to-room provenance, treatment documentation, and archive reconciliation rather than crime-story conventions. Preserve the six evidence dimensions and the checksum as the sole selection condition; do not encode the answer through name, job title, narrative order, or an opening reveal.
intended_answer: The premise deliberately does not identify the participant; the formalizer and deterministic evaluation must derive the unique match from the supplied evidence statuses and checksum rules.
premise: At the Bellwether Conservation Workshop, a salt-stained ceremonial panel is moved after a transport crate damages its painted surface. Its trail runs through Intake, the Imaging Room, the Solvent Bench, the Microscopy Room, and the Drying Vault. Five participants—an intake registrar, imaging technician, materials conservator, mount maker, and shift coordinator—leave overlapping entries in the room log, handling register, camera archive, treatment notes, and seal record. The incident docket evaluates each participant using six statuses: relational, temporal, causal, spatial, sequence, and protocol evidence. Each status is converted to its locally specified integer code, then folded in that order by the workshop checksum rule, h = (17h + code) mod 101, beginning with h = 0. The accepted result is the checksum recorded on the incident docket. In this workshop, “certified restoration lead” means the one participant whose six evidence statuses produce that accepted iterated modular checksum under the local rules.
setting_summary: A conservation workshop traces a damaged artifact through several rooms using overlapping records and six kinds of evidence. Five participants are candidates, while ordinary workflow details provide distractors without identifying any candidate.
target_question: Which participant has the six evidence statuses whose accepted iterated modular checksum matches under the workshop’s local rules?
